problem: Zero-shot VLM-based object navigation methods such as VLFM treat the environment as unknown for every query and store only query-specific similarity maps built from image-level features. They therefore cannot reuse earlier exploration for later objects, and their similarity maps are spatially imprecise.
motivation: Humans remember the semantic layout of a place and use it to find new objects faster, for example remembering where the kitchen is when looking for an oven. Real robots need a reusable, queryable semantic memory that runs in real time on board. Patch-level CLIP-aligned features with explicit modelling of depth and feature noise should give a more accurate map that supports both single-object and multi-object search.
key_idea: Build a persistent 2D open-vocabulary feature map (OneMap) from dense patch-level CLIP-aligned SED features, fused by recursive Bayesian (Kalman-style) updates with modelled observation uncertainty, and use its variance to drive frontier and revisit exploration across sequential queries.
insight: Storing features rather than per-query similarity lets the map be queried for any later object, and per-object SPL rises with the object index (35.08 -> 37.44 -> 46.01) while VLFM stays flat (27.50 / 32.61 / 29.13). Consensus-filtering between the detector and the map only works because the map is spatially accurate. Removing it drops SR from 55.8 to 48.2 and raises the false-positive rate from 19.5 to 26.6. OneMap still beats VLFM on SPL without it (31.2 vs 30.4), which supports the claim that the map itself is more informative.
method: Dense feature extraction: the SED ConvNeXt-based encoder gives per-patch CLIP-aligned features, which are bilinearly upsampled to pixel resolution.

Uncertainty model: pixel variance is the product of a feature-leakage term (tanh of the squared depth gradient) and a distance-based feature-extractor term (exp of the squared deviation from an optimal detection distance d_opt).

Projection and fusion into 2D: features are back-projected with depth and camera intrinsics, then projected to the map plane. Features in the same cell are combined by a weighted sum and their variances are averaged.
Depth-noise blur: a custom GPU sparse inverse Gaussian convolution blurs features with a variance quadratic in distance (sigma_d^2 = p d^2), following a stereo accuracy model.
Bayesian map update: each cell's feature and variance are fused into the persistent map with a Kalman gain, giving a belief map of features and variances (about 700 MB for 50x50 m at 10 cells/m).

Query and sub-maps: the CLIP text embedding is compared by cosine similarity with every cell. Observed, semantically explored (thresholded variance), searched (a separate variance sigma_E reset on each new query) and navigable maps are kept.

Goal selection and detection: frontiers between the explored and observed maps are scored by the maximum similarity in the reachable unexplored area, and high-similarity clusters in E-C are scored likewise. The best goal is chosen greedily and planned with A*. A detection counts only if YOLOv7 (or YOLO-World) fires and the map similarity is in the top 5 percentile (consensus filtering).

setting.backbone: SED (ConvNeXt + CLIP, pretrained, frozen) + CLIP text encoder + YOLOv7 / YOLO-World detector; no navigation policy is trained
setting.training_data: none (training-free; uses pretrained SED, CLIP and detectors)
setting.action_space: A* path on a 2D grid to the selected frontier or goal, executed by a path-tracking controller; no learned locomotion

numbers.extra: single-object; Habitat ObjectNav challenge validation split, 2000 episodes; no locomotion or semantic training

results: On HM3D single-object ObjectNav, OneMap reaches SPL 37.4 and SR 55.8, beating the zero-shot baselines VLFM (30.4 / 52.5) and ESC (22.3 / 39.2), and beating PIRLNav's SPL (27.1) though not its SR (64.1). On the new multi-object benchmark it gets SR 54.24, SPL 27.77 and PR 65.54 vs VLFM's 44.92, 19.90 and 57.34. The gap widens for later goals in the sequence, and the system runs at 2 Hz on a Jetson Orin AGX on a Spot robot.
limitations: The map is 2D, and depth noise still affects feature localization; 3D representations are left to future work.
The multi-object benchmark is small (236 episodes, 3 goals, 6 categories) and is compared only against VLFM; outdoor scenes and less meaningful semantics are untested.
Real-world evaluation is only qualitative, with no quantitative results; the depth-noise parameter had to be retuned for the real robot.
